messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL exactly matches the DOI given in the source metadata and citation: 10.1016/j.envpol.2024.125201 / https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envpol.2024.125201.
Author list, title, journal, year, volume, and article number all match the provided source citation text.

S01-E05 states they "sampled a representative surface water (drinking water source) in Beijing, China" and used it in bench-scale treatment tests; S01-E02 and S01-E06 discuss algae in the water. This supports that the matrix is representative surface water with natural algae and organic matter used as raw water for coagulation, simulated sand filtration, and UF.

S01-E06 notes PFAS effects were evaluated on coagulation, filtration and ultrafiltration processes in DWTP. S01-E02 mentions "coagulation, simulated sand filtration, and UF" and defines a control filtered by MF membrane. Together these support the described conventional treatment sequence and inclusion of an MF membrane control.

S01-E05 states that they "dosed 2 representative PFAS compounds... to conduct bench-scale treatment tests" on representative surface water from Beijing, supporting that the study was bench-scale using that surface water through the coagulation–filtration–UF train.

S01-E06 identifies potassium perfluorooctanesulfonate (PFOS) as one of two PFAS used and says stock solutions were prepared and added into surface water samples; S01-E04 refers to PFAS concentrations of 0.1, 1, and 10 μg/L in PFOA solutions, and the paper context applies these levels for both PFOS and PFOA. Combined, the evidence supports PFOS addition to surface water at 0.1, 1, and 10 μg/L.

S01-E06 identifies sodium perfluorooctanoate (PFOA) as the second PFAS used with stock solutions prepared and added into surface water samples; S01-E04 explicitly cites PFAS concentrations of 0.1, 1, and 10 μg/L in the PFOA solutions. This supports the stated PFOA scope and concentration levels.
S01-E04 reports effects "under PFAS concentrations of 0.1, 1, and 10 μg/L," matching the listed values "0.1, 1, and 10".
S01-E04 gives the PFAS levels in "μg/L", matching the unit recorded for the PFAS concentration levels tested.

S01-E06 states "Polyaluminum chloride (PACl... ) [SOURCE_TEXT_OMITTED sha256=70c0d36e02e86bb6f957b9d435b6ce9f2df01d61dd904b1ec5c0fa1be6c95886]," supporting PACl as the coagulant type and its preparation described in the qualifiers.
S01-E06 specifies that "Each stock solution of PFAS was prepared using deionized (DI) water at a concentration of 100 mg/L," matching the value 100.
S01-E06 gives the PFAS stock solution concentration in mg/L, matching the recorded unit.

S01-E02 defines the control as "JM samples filtered by MF membrane, with algae addition but without additional PFAS dose," which supports the description of a PFAS-free surface water control (with algae and treatment but no added PFAS).

This endpoint concerns floc size during coagulation, which is not a removal, destruction, or flux metric; classifying it as endpoint_type "other" is consistent with the measurement basis described in S01-E05 and S01-E08.

S01-E05 reports that "the presence of PFAS caused larger flocs during coagulation" and that at 0.1 μg/L PFAS there was the greatest influence on floc growth. S01-E08 reiterates that PFOS and PFOA contamination leads to larger-size flocs. This supports the interpretation of increased floc size at low PFAS concentration compared with PFAS-free control.
The endpoint describes UF membrane flux decline/fouling, a physical separation performance measure. Classifying it as "separation" matches the UF filtration context in S01-E02, S01-E05, and S01-E08.

S01-E05 states that PFAS presence caused "more severe ultrafiltration (UF) membrane fouling" and that at 0.1 μg/L PFAS, membrane flux declined more than 10% relative to the PFAS-free solution. S01-E02 and S01-E08 discuss UF performance under PFAS contamination. This supports the interpretation of stronger UF flux decline in PFAS-dosed conditions, greatest at 0.1 μg/L.
S01-E05 specifies that at 0.1 μg/L PFAS, "the floc size increased by 1.6 times" compared with the solution without PFAS, matching the recorded value 1.6 as an exact numeric fold-change.
The source (S01-E05) expresses the change as "increased by 1.6 times," a fold-change; representing this with unit "fold" is appropriate and consistent.
S01-E05 states that at 0.1 μg/L PFAS, "membrane flux declined more than 10%," which is correctly captured as the inequality value ">10" with value_form "inequality."
S01-E05 gives the decline as a percentage ("more than 10%"), so the unit "%" is correct.

S01-E05 describes bench-scale treatment tests on a representative surface water from Beijing with two PFAS; S01-E06 limits the chemicals to PFOS and PFOA and describes the DWTP processes tested. From these design facts, it reasonably follows (design-inferred) that results may not generalize to other water matrices, PFAS species, or full-scale operations.

The cited excerpts (S01-E01, S01-E02, S01-E05, S01-E06) describe aims, PFAS dosing, treatment processes, and algae responses but do not state that PFAS removal, transformation, or degradation products were not reported. Inferring non-reporting from these limited sections is not strictly supported by the provided text.

S01-E05 concludes that the observed [SOURCE_TEXT_OMITTED sha256=40ff0c7174f9bfdfd2245e0418627178af98cea68d2d6f014e4a277d2c53181a]." S01-E07 and S01-E08 likewise attribute treatment changes to algae stress and biopolymer production. This supports the author-reported mechanism statement.

S01-E05 notes bench-scale tests on the same representative surface water with and without PFAS. S01-E02 defines the MF control with algae but no added PFAS. PFAS concentration was systematically varied at environmental levels (S01-E04, S01-E05), while the treatment train remained the same (S01-E02, S01-E06). These design details justify classifying PFAS-dosed vs PFAS-free conditions as comparable_with_conditions.

The reasoning that PFAS-dosed and PFAS-free treatments share the same surface water matrix and treatment sequence, differing mainly in PFAS concentration, is consistent with descriptions in S01-E02, S01-E05, and S01-E06, enabling controlled comparison of floc size and UF flux decline.

result.record_usable_rationale: Core elements—source identity, matrix, PFAS identity and concentration, treatment configuration, control vs PFAS-dosed comparability, endpoints, and quantitative findings—are all supported by the cited text and correctly transcribed. One residuals/byproducts limitation about lack of PFAS removal/degradation reporting is unsupported but does not affect use of the record for PFAS treatment performance and matrix-effect analysis.
